extracted.intended_audience: the people/citizens (specifically People of the State of New York) and readers concerned with constitutional design and federal-state taxation powers
extracted.subtask_description: A late-18th-century Federalist essay arguing principles for interpreting the proposed U.S. Constitution's taxation, necessary-and-proper, and supremacy clauses, and for allocating fiscal powers between the Union and the States. The text defends concurrent federal/state taxing authority (except for duties on imports/exports) and explains interpretive rules for exclusive delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer usurpation concerns to composition and structure of government
rubrics_metrics.description: All observations founded upon the danger of usurpation ought to be referred to the composition and structure of the government, not to the nature or extent of its powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid speculative conjectures about hypothetical usurpations; evaluate risk of usurpation by examining how the government is constituted and how officeholders depend on the people. Anti-pattern: launching into imaginative scenarios of federal usurpation without analyzing institutional safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: States retain complete sovereignty except where exclusively delegated
rubrics_metrics.description: The State governments... are invested with complete sovereignty... they would clearly retain all the rights of sovereignty which they before had, and which were not, by that act, EXCLUSIVELY delegated to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret grants to the Union as limited; unless the Constitution shows exclusive delegation, states keep their preexisting authorities. Use the instrument's text and structure to identify explicit divestitures of state sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three cases of exclusive delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive delegation (alienation of State sovereignty) exists where: (1) the Constitution in express terms granted an exclusive authority to the Union; (2) it granted in one instance an authority to the Union, and in another prohibited the States from exercising the like authority; (3) it granted an authority to the Union to which a similar authority in the States would be absolutely and totally contradictory and repugnant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these three structural tests when deciding whether a power is exclusive. Examples given: exclusive legislation over the federal district (case 1); duties on imports/exports where prohibition against state imposts implies federal exclusivity (case 2); uniform rule of naturalization where differing state rules would defeat uniformity (case 3). Distinguish true constitutional repugnancy from mere policy interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative pregnant indicates concurrent state authority for other taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The restriction that 'NO STATE SHALL, without the consent of Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports' amounts to a NEGATIVE PREGNANT — a negation of one thing, and an affirmation of another (i.e., that states retain authority to tax other articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of express prohibitions in the Constitution (negative clauses) as interpretive signals that omitted authorities were intentionally left with the States. Anti-pattern: treating the prohibition as implying that states' other taxing powers are subordinate to the national legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to tax internal articles is concurrent, not exclusive to Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of imposing taxes on all articles other than exports and imports... is manifestly a concurrent and coequal authority in the United States and in the individual States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the taxing clause in light of the lack of express exclusive language; absent explicit exclusion, assume concurrency. Consider practical implications but recognize that policy conflicts are matters of prudence, not constitutional extinguishment of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and Proper clause is declaratory of an implied truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause authorizing Congress to make all laws which shall be NECESSARY and PROPER for carrying into execution the powers vested... is only declaratory of a truth which would have resulted by necessary and unavoidable implication from constituting a federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the Necessary and Proper clause as confirming that means to execute granted powers (e.g., laws to collect taxes) are included; it does not itself enlarge substantive powers beyond those granted. Anti-pattern: viewing the clause as an independent license to create new substantive powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative powers include the means necessary to execute them
rubrics_metrics.description: A power to lay and collect taxes must be a power to pass all laws NECESSARY and PROPER for the execution of that power; legislative power is a power of making laws, and the proper means to execute that power are laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a legislative power, include reasonable laws that effectuate that power. Use this line of reasoning to justify laws instrumental to carrying out enumerated powers (e.g., tax collection mechanisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy clause applies only to laws made pursuant to the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution... expressly confines this supremacy to laws made PURSUANT TO THE CONSTITUTION; acts not pursuant to its constitutional powers are merely acts of usurpation and not the supreme law of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a federal act exceeds constitutional powers, categorize it as usurpation and not binding simply because of the supremacy clause. The supremacy claim must be read together with the limitation 'pursuant to the Constitution.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Who judges necessity/propriety: government first, people ultimately
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government... must judge, in the first instance, of the proper exercise of its powers, and its constituents in the last. If the federal government overpasses its authority, the people must appeal to the standard they have formed and take measures the exigency suggests and prudence justifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a two-tiered accountability: routine determinations by the federal branches, with ultimate political remedy and constitutional correction resting with the people. Legal/political recourse is available for overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy conflicts do not equal constitutional repugnancy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax laid by a State which might render it INEXPEDIENT that thus a further tax should be laid on the same article by the Union... would not imply a constitutional inability to impose a further tax; quantity and expediency are questions of prudence, not of exclusive constitutional authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between conflicts of policy/expediency (which call for mutual forbearance or political accommodation) and direct constitutional contradiction (which can imply exclusion). Do not infer extinguishment of power from mere imprudence or inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction in taxation follows from division of sovereign power and instrument's tenor
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of a concurrent jurisdiction in certain cases results from the division of the sovereign power; the rule that all authorities of which the States are not explicitly divested... remain with them in full vigor is clearly admitted by the whole tenor of the instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Constitution's overall structure — including numerous negative clauses — to interpret whether authorities remain with states. The presence of targeted prohibitions supports the inference of retained concurrent state powers elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricting federal taxation to particular objects produces unequal burdens and economic harms
rubrics_metrics.description: If the jurisdiction of the national government in the article of revenue should be restricted to particular objects, it would naturally occasion an undue proportion of the public burdens to fall upon those objects: oppression of particular branches of industry; an unequal distribution of the taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals limiting federal funds (e.g., to import duties) by their distributional and economic effects: excessive duties risk smuggling, market distortions, monopolies for certain manufacturing classes, and merchants bearing burdens. Consider practical consequences, not only abstract fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions must provide capacity for future contingencies (esp. defense), not only present exigencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions of civil government are not to be framed upon a calculation of existing exigencies... There ought to be a CAPACITY to provide for future contingencies as they may happen; and as these are illimitable in their nature, it is impossible safely to limit that capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When allocating taxing authority, account for unpredictable future needs (national defense, wars, debts). Narrow, short-sighted fiscal delimitations risk leaving the Union unable to perform essential functions in future contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction preferable to exclusive subordination for balancing Union and State interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A CONCURRENT JURISDICTION in the article of taxation was the only admissible substitute for an entire subordination, in respect to this branch of power, of State authority to that of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concurrency as a pragmatic compromise: it reconciles an indefinite federal taxing capacity with adequate and independent state power to provide for local necessities. Beware proposals that grant exclusive long-term fiscal sources to states beyond what their probable needs justify.
